newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Wall to protect U.S. troops blocked in Sarajevo.
newsitem.headline: Wall to protect U.S. troops blocked in Sarajevo.

text.p: U.S. officers said on Sunday that Sarajevo city authorities and a handful of demonstrators have blocked the erection of a protective wall around new quarters being prepared for American troops in Sarajevo.

Foundations for the 15-foot-high blast barrier were being laid in the street outside the new quarters on Saturday when a government television crew and several angry women showed up to block the project.

"I'd say it wasn't spontaneous because the police and a front-end loader and a water truck arrived on the scene with the women and they pushed our work out of the street, cleared it all away," U.S. Army Major Bob Hammons said.
"I can tell you we will not occupy this building unless the walls are up to offer a measure of protection to American soldiers.
"The leadership will not risk their lives. This is a U.S. issue not a (NATO) issue," Hammons told Reuters.
No city officials were available for comment on Sunday.
Hammons, chief of the U.S. National Support Element in Sarajevo, has spent about $300,000 fixing up part of a 19th century factory building in Sarajevo's old town.
The project is intended to provide finance, postal and administrative support for U.S. troops serving in Bosnia's peace force and living quarters for about 50 American soldiers.
Hammons said that Bosnian Interior Ministry officials had approved the blast barrier but the project was bogged down in municipal bureaucracy, which had not yet issued a permit.
Since a truck bomb killed 19 American soldiers and wounded nearly 400 in Saudi Arabia in June, such blast barriers have become indispensable in U.S. military eyes.
"There's a significant Iranian presence here in Sarajevo and Bosnia," Hammons said. "We must protect our men and women."

U.S. government officials have been lobbying the Bosnian government and its ruling Party of Democratic Action (SDA) leadership to sever all ties with Iran, which Washington views as posing a potential terrorist threat.
SDA leaders are well-disposed to Iran because it supplied desperately needed arms to Bosnia during the war and the Serb siege of Sarajevo.
Some local residents of the area said they feared the entire street in front of the building would be blocked by the wall. U.S. officers said the street would not be obstructed.

Bosnian Serb media alleged that the barrier was being erected to protect Momcilo Krajisnik, a Serb recently elected to Bosnia's three-man collective presidency and expected soon in Sarajevo for an inaugural meeting.
U.S. and NATO sources dismissed that report as "nonsense".
